items.followUp: Define biological catalysts and state one property of enzymes.

rubric.why: Identifies enzymes as catalysts that act in living systems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzymes are biological catalysts or that they speed up reactions in living organisms.

rubric.why: Shows that enzymes can act repeatedly after a reaction.
rubric.description: States that enzymes are not used up or permanently changed in the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzymes remain unchanged or are not consumed by the reaction.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
They are not used up or permanently changed during the reactions they catalyse.

items.followUp: What is an enzyme, and what happens to it during the reaction it catalyses?

rubric.why: Defines metabolism as the totality of chemical reactions in the organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing metabolism as the sum or total of the chemical reactions occurring in an organism or its cells.

rubric.why: States why metabolism is essential for life.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking metabolism to obtaining energy or to growth, repair, or maintenance of the body.

modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions taking place in an organism or its cells.
These reactions provide energy and materials needed for growth, repair, and maintenance of the body.

items.followUp: How does light intensity affect the rate of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Identifies the initial effect of increasing carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.description: Explains that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a rise in carbon dioxide concentration increases the photosynthetic rate, at least initially.

rubric.why: Recognises that carbon dioxide is not the only factor controlling photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Describes the limit to the effect of increasing carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate eventually levels off or reaches a maximum when another factor becomes limiting.

modelAnswer: As the concentration of carbon dioxide increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases, provided other factors are adequate.
The rate eventually levels off because another factor becomes limiting.

items.followUp: What is alcoholic fermentation, and what are its products?

rubric.why: Identifies the process as an anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: States that lactic acid fermentation takes place without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the process as anaerobic or stating that it occurs in the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: Names the characteristic product of this type of fermentation.
rubric.description: Names lactic acid as the product of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming lactic acid as a product; energy release may also be mentioned.

modelAnswer: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, occurring when oxygen is unavailable.
It produces lactic acid and releases a small amount of energy.

items.followUp: State one role of fermentation in food production and one situation in which it occurs in the human body.

rubric.why: Identifies fermentation as a way to release some energy when oxygen is insufficient.
rubric.description: States the role of fermentation in muscles when oxygen is limited.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that muscle cells can release energy by anaerobic respiration when oxygen is insufficient, producing lactic acid.

rubric.why: Gives a practical use of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct use such as bread-making or producing alcoholic drinks.

modelAnswer: When the oxygen supply to muscles is insufficient, anaerobic respiration releases some energy and produces lactic acid.
Fermentation by microorganisms is used in food production, for example in bread-making and brewing alcoholic drinks.

items.followUp: Explain how a pressure difference helps move sugars through the phloem.

rubric.why: Identifies the region where sugars enter the phloem and pressure rises.
rubric.description: Describes sugar loading at the source and the resulting rise in pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugars are loaded into the phloem at the source, causing water to enter and pressure to rise.

rubric.why: Explains that a pressure difference drives movement towards the sink.
rubric.description: Defines pressure flow as movement of phloem sap down a pressure gradient from source to sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing movement from the high-pressure source towards the lower-pressure sink.

modelAnswer: The pressure flow mechanism is the movement of food through the phloem from a source to a sink due to a pressure difference.
Sugars loaded at the source cause water to enter the phloem, raising pressure; sap then flows towards the lower-pressure sink.

items.followUp: Compare unicellular and multicellular organisms, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Describes the first type of cellular organization and its basic feature.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that a unicellular organism consists of one cell, and 1 for a correct example such as Amoeba, a bacterium, or yeast.

rubric.why: Describes the second type and distinguishes its organization from that of unicellular organisms.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that a multicellular organism consists of many cells, and 1 for a correct example such as a plant or animal. Credit may be given for noting that its cells are specialized.

modelAnswer: Organisms are classified by their cellular organization as unicellular or multicellular.
Unicellular organisms consist of a single cell, which carries out all life processes; examples include Amoeba and bacteria.
Multicellular organisms consist of many cells; examples include plants and animals.
In many multicellular organisms, cells are specialized to perform different functions.

items.followUp: Describe the structure of the nucleus and state its main functions.

rubric.why: Describes the boundary of the nucleus and how it communicates with the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that the nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane or envelope, and 1 for mentioning pores in it.

rubric.why: Identifies important contents of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for correctly naming or describing nuclear contents, such as nucleoplasm, chromatin/chromosomes containing DNA, and the nucleolus.

rubric.why: States a key function of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives the function of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the nucleus controls cell activities or contains hereditary information passed to daughter cells.

modelAnswer: The nucleus is usually a prominent organelle in the cell and is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane with pores.
It contains nucleoplasm, in which the nucleolus and chromatin are present.
Chromatin contains DNA and forms chromosomes during cell division; genes on DNA carry hereditary information.
The nucleus controls the activities of the cell and transmits hereditary information.
